query: For high-entropy alloys, what single intervention could improve dynamic strength–ductility performance? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an untreated baseline, defines the boundary conditions under which it should hold, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a decisive experiment that could falsify it.

generation.target_system: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) with improved dynamic strength-ductility performance

generation.hypothesis: The addition of specific alloying elements, such as Cr, and interstitial doping can improve the dynamic strength-ductility performance of high-entropy alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast or wrought high-entropy alloy with a specific composition
generation.intervention: Addition of alloying elements (e.g., Cr) and/or interstitial doping (e.g., with oxygen or nitrogen)
generation.conditions: Room temperature or elevated temperatures, depending on the specific application
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a Laves phase or ordered interstitial complexes
generation.mechanism: Solid solution hardening, grain boundary strengthening, and lattice distortion, as well as the formation of a continuous reticulated structure of the Laves phase, which hinders crack propagation and compensates for the plasticity loss typically caused by brittle intermetallics.
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and ductility, as well as enhanced dynamic strength-ductility performance
generation.baseline: Untreated high-entropy alloy with a similar composition
generation.boundary: The intervention is expected to be effective within a specific range of temperatures and strain rates, depending on the alloy composition and processing route
generation.uncertainty: The exact mechanisms and effects of the intervention may vary depending on the specific alloy composition, processing route, and testing conditions

falsification_experiment.design: Tensile testing and microstructural analysis of treated and untreated high-entropy alloys
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated alloy does not exhibit improved dynamic strength-ductility performance compared to the untreated alloy, the hypothesis is falsified.

Question: How does the addition of Cr to the HfMoTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy affect its phase composition, microstructure, and room-temperature mechanical properties, specifically regarding the synergy between strength and ductility?. System: HfMoTaTiZr (30.0 at% Hf, 16.1 at% Mo, 30.4 at% Ta, 8.1 at% Ti, 15.4 at% Zr) and HfMoTaTiZrCr0.5 (28.8 at% Hf, 15.5 at% Mo, 29.1 at% Ta, 7.7 at% Ti, 14.7 at% Zr, 4.2 at% Cr). Processing: Vacuum arc melting in an inert gas atmosphere; ingots re-melted at least 5 times to improve chemical homogeneity; weight loss did not exceed 0.5 wt%. Test conditions: Room temperature; Vickers hardness with 0.3 kg load and 15 s dwelling time; compression tests on cylindrical samples (3 mm diameter, 6 mm height) at a ram speed of 0.008 mm s−1 (strain rate 0.001/s). Findings: The addition of 4.2 at% Cr led to the formation of a Laves phase in addition to the BCC phase, whereas the base alloy was single-phase BCC.; The hardness of HfMoTaTiZrCr0.5 reached 535.8 Hv0.3, which is 56.96% higher than the reference alloy HfMoTaTiZr (460.1 Hv0.3).; The yield strength of HfMoTaTiZrCr0.5 reached 1750.6 ± 80.3 MPa, which is 207.5 MPa higher than HfMoTaTi

Paper card. Question: Can high-entropy alloys be designed to simultaneously achieve high Snoek-type damping capacity, high mechanical strength, and high ductility at elevated temperatures?. System: Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi base HEA, (Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi)98O2 (O-2 HEA), and (Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi)98N2 (N-2 HEA). Processing: Arc-melting of pure metals (purity >99.9 wt%), TiN (99.9 wt%), and TiO2 (99.9 wt%) in a Ti-gettered high-purity argon atmosphere; remelted at least eight times; drop-cast into a water-cooled copper mold (10 mm × 10 mm × 60 mm). Test conditions: Damping measured via multifunction internal friction apparatus at 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, and 4.0 Hz, temperature range 300–1100 K, heating rate 2 K min⁻¹, max strain amplitude 2 × 10⁻⁴; Tensile tests at room temperature, strain rate 1 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹. Findings: The O-2 HEA achieved a peak damping capacity (tanδ_max) of 0.020 at 1.0 Hz, while the N-2 HEA reached 0.027 at 1.0 Hz.; The N-2 HEA exhibited a yield strength of 1362 MPa and elongation of ~11.9%, while the O-2 HEA showed 1138 MPa yield strength and ~20% elongation.; The peak damping temperature (T_p) for the HEAs was approximately 730–747 K at 1.0 Hz, roughly 100 K higher than traditional Snoe
